Lab 5: Following the Money

84-355 Democracy’s Data | Week 5

Your name here

August 03, 2026

Before we start

Chapter 4 asks who pays for campaigns and what they get for it. Today we open the actual ledger.

Every federal candidate must report to the Federal Election Commission: what came in, what went out, and — crucially — who it came from. That last column is where this lab lives. It is easy to ask how much money is in politics. It is much more interesting to ask whose money goes to whom, and today you can answer that precisely.

Everything is base R. Work in order.

Part 1: The ledger

fec <- read.csv("data/fec_candidates_2024.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(fec)
#> [1] 3856   18

Nearly four thousand candidates for federal office in the 2023–24 cycle. One row each.

head(fec[, c("cand_name", "office", "office_st", "ici", "party",
             "ttl_receipts", "indiv_contrib", "pac_contrib")], 4)
#>        cand_name office office_st ici party ttl_receipts indiv_contrib
#> 1 GALLEGO, RUBEN  House        AZ   I   DEM     64657200    59385707.3
#> 2   TRONE, DAVID  House        MD   I   DEM     63833137      853811.6
#> 3   SCHIFF, ADAM  House        CA   I   DEM     48149197    45110628.7
#> 4   ROSEN, JACKY  House        NV   I   DEM     43915245    33769624.6
#>   pac_contrib
#> 1     1784685
#> 2        5000
#> 3     1015453
#> 4     2574528

The columns that matter today:

  • ttl_receipts — everything the campaign took in
  • indiv_contrib — money from individual people
  • pac_contrib — money from political action committees
  • party_contrib — money from the party
  • self_funding — money the candidate gave or lent their own campaign
  • ici — Incumbent, Challenger, or Open seat

That last one is the most important variable in the file, and you will see why shortly.

table(fec$office)
#> 
#>     House President    Senate 
#>      3073       174       609
table(fec$ici)
#> 
#>         C    I    O 
#>   60 2183  673  940

Part 2: The shape of the money

Start with the House, because there are enough candidates for the pattern to be clear.

h <- fec[fec$office == "House", ]
nrow(h)
#> [1] 3073

What does a typical House candidate raise?

round(median(h$ttl_receipts))
#> [1] 22583
round(mean(h$ttl_receipts))
#> [1] 782177

Stop and look at those two numbers. The median House candidate raised about $22,600. The average House candidate raised about $782,000 — nearly thirty-five times more. Whenever a mean is that far above a median, a small number of cases are carrying almost everything.

How far does it go?

r <- sort(h$ttl_receipts, decreasing = TRUE)
top10 <- round(0.10 * length(r))

round(100 * sum(r[1:top10]) / sum(r), 1)                     # top 10% of candidates
#> [1] 72.7
round(100 * sum(r[(round(0.5 * length(r)) + 1):length(r)]) / sum(r), 1)   # bottom 50%
#> [1] 0.2

The best-funded tenth of House candidates raised 72.7% of all House money. The bottom half raised 0.2% — two tenths of one percent, split between more than fifteen hundred people.

plot(seq_along(r) / length(r) * 100, cumsum(r) / sum(r) * 100, type = "l",
     lwd = 2.5, col = "#2166AC",
     xlab = "Candidates, best-funded first (%)",
     ylab = "Share of all House money raised (%)",
     main = "Almost all the money is with almost none of the candidates")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
abline(v = 10, lty = 3, col = "grey40")

The dashed diagonal is what perfect equality would look like. We are nowhere near it.

Part 3: Incumbents and everyone else

Now split by whether the candidate already holds the seat.

hs <- h[h$ici %in% c("I", "C", "O"), ]
aggregate(ttl_receipts ~ ici, data = hs, FUN = median)
#>   ici ttl_receipts
#> 1   C     9106.745
#> 2   I  1537104.825
#> 3   O    19272.080
meds <- aggregate(ttl_receipts ~ ici, data = hs, FUN = median)
meds <- meds[match(c("C", "O", "I"), meds$ici), ]

bp <- barplot(meds$ttl_receipts / 1000,
        names.arg = c("Challenger", "Open seat", "Incumbent"),
        col = c("#B2182B", "#999999", "#2166AC"), border = NA,
        ylab = "Median receipts ($ thousands)",
        main = "What a typical House candidate raises")
text(bp, meds$ttl_receipts / 1000, labels = paste0("$", round(meds$ttl_receipts / 1000)),
     pos = 3, xpd = TRUE, cex = 0.9)

The median incumbent raised $1,537,105. The median challenger raised $9,107. That is a ratio of about 169 to 1.

Before concluding anything, note what this cannot distinguish. Incumbents might raise more because incumbency attracts money, or the people who attract money might be the ones who become incumbents. Both stories fit this chart.

The next part separates them.

Part 4: Whose money?

Here is the question the ledger can actually settle. Take every serious House campaign — say, everyone who raised more than $50,000 — and ask what share of their money came from PACs rather than individuals.

ser <- hs[hs$ttl_receipts > 50000, ]
ser$pac_share <- 100 * ser$pac_contrib / ser$ttl_receipts

aggregate(pac_share ~ ici, data = ser, FUN = function(x) round(median(x), 1))
#>   ici pac_share
#> 1   C       1.1
#> 2   I      37.6
#> 3   O       1.4
ps <- aggregate(pac_share ~ ici, data = ser, FUN = median)
ps <- ps[match(c("C", "O", "I"), ps$ici), ]

bp <- barplot(ps$pac_share, names.arg = c("Challenger", "Open seat", "Incumbent"),
        col = c("#B2182B", "#999999", "#2166AC"), border = NA, ylim = c(0, 45),
        ylab = "PAC share of receipts (%), median",
        main = "Where PAC money goes")
text(bp, ps$pac_share, labels = paste0(round(ps$pac_share, 1), "%"),
     pos = 3, xpd = TRUE, cex = 0.95)

This is the finding of the lab. For a typical serious House incumbent, 37.6% of all money raised came from PACs. For a challenger running just as serious a campaign, the figure is 1.1%. For an open seat, 1.4%.

Individuals give to candidates they like. PACs give to people who already hold power — and they are not subtle about it. An open-seat candidate has just as much chance of winning as an incumbent’s challenger does of losing, and PACs fund neither.

This is why the incumbency gap in Part 3 is not simply “good candidates attract money.” Organised money is choosing by office held, not by quality, competitive­ ness, or ideology.

Part 5: Buying your own campaign

Some candidates skip donors entirely.

big <- fec[fec$ttl_receipts > 100000, ]
big$self_pct <- 100 * big$self_funding / big$ttl_receipts

sum(big$self_pct > 50)
#> [1] 225
nrow(big)
#> [1] 1421
head(fec[order(-fec$self_funding),
         c("cand_name", "office", "party", "ttl_receipts", "self_funding")], 6)
#>                     cand_name    office party ttl_receipts self_funding
#> 2                TRONE, DAVID     House   DEM     63833137     62877800
#> 3253             TRONE, DAVID    Senate   DEM     63833137     62877800
#> 3077         RAMASWAMY, VIVEK President   REP     66197196     54755270
#> 3080           JOHNSON, PERRY President   REP     29704589     29364171
#> 3259          SCOTT, RICK SEN    Senate   REP     36696093     21393850
#> 3079 NORRIS, JIM ALEXANDER SR President   REP     35430000     20950000

Of the 1,421 candidates who raised over $100,000, 225 — about one in six — put up more than half of it themselves.

Part 6: The trap in this file

Look at the two best-funded candidates in the entire dataset:

fec[grepl("HARRIS, KAMALA|BIDEN, JOSEPH", fec$cand_name),
    c("cand_id", "cand_name", "ttl_receipts", "indiv_contrib")]
#>        cand_id          cand_name ttl_receipts indiv_contrib
#> 3074 P00009423     HARRIS, KAMALA   1175189365     613557357
#> 3075 P80000722 BIDEN, JOSEPH R JR   1175189365     613557357

Those are the same dollars. Biden’s presidential committee became Harris’s when he withdrew in July 2024. The FEC carries two candidate records — different IDs, different names, one pile of money — and reports the full $1,175,189,365 against each.

It is not only the presidential race:

b <- fec[fec$ttl_receipts > 1e6, ]
d <- table(b$ttl_receipts)
shared <- as.numeric(names(d[d > 1]))

head(b[b$ttl_receipts %in% shared,
       c("cand_id", "cand_name", "office", "office_st", "ttl_receipts")], 10)
#>      cand_id              cand_name office office_st ttl_receipts
#> 1  H4AZ07043         GALLEGO, RUBEN  House        AZ     64657200
#> 2  H6MD08549           TRONE, DAVID  House        MD     63833137
#> 3  H0CA27085           SCHIFF, ADAM  House        CA     48149197
#> 4  H6NV03139           ROSEN, JACKY  House        NV     43915245
#> 13 H2TN06030 BLACKBURN, MARSHA MRS.  House        TN     13571274
#> 17 H8NJ03206              KIM, ANDY  House        NJ     12441004
#> 20 H8NM01224       HEINRICH, MARTIN  House        NM     10731410
#> 29 H2VA10240              CAO, HUNG  House        VA      9832460
#> 77 H2WI03130         COOKE, REBECCA  House        WI      6358059
#> 78 H4WI03169         COOKE, REBECCA  House        WI      6358059

Ruben Gallego, David Trone, Adam Schiff and Jacky Rosen each appear twice — once as a House candidate and once as a Senate candidate — because each ran for the Senate in 2024 and moved their committee money across. Eric Hovde appears twice under two candidate IDs for the same Senate race.

How much does this matter?

round(sum(fec$ttl_receipts) / 1e6)
#> [1] 6846
nodup <- fec[!duplicated(fec$ttl_receipts) | fec$ttl_receipts == 0, ]
round(sum(nodup$ttl_receipts) / 1e6)
#> [1] 5275

Add up the column naively and you get $6.85 billion raised in the 2024 cycle. Strip out the repeated totals and you get about $5.27 billion. The difference — roughly $1.6 billion — is money that does not exist. It is the same money, counted twice.

Note that the second number is a rough correction, not a right answer: dropping every repeated value would also drop two genuinely different candidates who happened to raise exactly the same amount. It is good enough to show you the size of the problem, and not good enough to publish. Knowing the difference between those two standards is most of what this course is about.

Part 7: What this file cannot tell you

The FEC’s file layout has a column for whether the candidate won the general election. Here is how much of it is filled in:

"gen_election" %in% names(fec)
#> [1] FALSE

The column is not in our file because it is empty in the source — all 3,856 rows of it. The FEC collects money, not results. It is a regulator of finance, not an election administrator, and as you learned in Week 2, the United States does not have one of those.

So the most obvious question in this whole subject — does the candidate who raises more money win? — cannot be answered with campaign finance data alone. You would have to go and find election results from fifty-one separate authorities and join them on, and then you would be doing Week 2’s lab again, with all of Week 2’s problems.

This is not a gap in our dataset. It is a fact about how the American state keeps its books.

What you can say from this file is nonetheless substantial: the money is extraordinarily concentrated, it flows overwhelmingly to people who already hold office, and the organised part of it flows almost nowhere else.

Part 8: On your own

This is the part you turn in. You are not being asked to write code. Each option is a working chunk with one thing to change, or nothing at all.

Pick one.

Option A — Does the Senate work the same way?

Everything above used the House. Change one word and find out.

which_office <- "Senate"          # <- change to "House" or "President"

o <- fec[fec$office == which_office & fec$ici %in% c("I", "C", "O"), ]
o <- o[o$ttl_receipts > 50000, ]
o$pac_share <- 100 * o$pac_contrib / o$ttl_receipts

aggregate(pac_share ~ ici, data = o, FUN = function(x) round(median(x), 1))
#>   ici pac_share
#> 1   C       0.2
#> 2   I      15.0
#> 3   O       0.7
aggregate(ttl_receipts ~ ici, data = o, FUN = function(x) round(median(x)))
#>   ici ttl_receipts
#> 1   C       574755
#> 2   I      2845748
#> 3   O       947895
table(o$ici)
#> 
#>   C   I   O 
#>  80 102  66

Write about: the same pattern appears, but the PAC gap is much smaller in the Senate — around 15% for incumbents against under 1% for challengers, rather than 37.6% against 1.1%. Suggest why. Senate races are far more expensive and far more often competitive; does either fact help explain a smaller PAC share? Think about what a PAC’s maximum contribution is worth as a fraction of a $90 million campaign versus a $2 million one.

Option B — Where does the money come from?

min_raised <- 50000               # <- change this threshold

s <- fec[fec$office == "House" & fec$ici %in% c("I","C","O") &
         fec$ttl_receipts > min_raised, ]

src <- sapply(c("C","O","I"), function(k) {
  x <- s[s$ici == k, ]
  c(Individuals = sum(x$indiv_contrib), PACs = sum(x$pac_contrib),
    Party = sum(x$party_contrib), Self = sum(x$self_funding)) / sum(x$ttl_receipts) * 100
})
colnames(src) <- c("Challenger", "Open seat", "Incumbent")
round(src, 1)
#>             Challenger Open seat Incumbent
#> Individuals       68.1      62.7      57.9
#> PACs               7.6       7.5      24.5
#> Party              0.2       0.1       0.1
#> Self              17.4      25.8       4.8
barplot(src, beside = FALSE, col = c("#2166AC", "#B2182B", "#999999", "#F4A582"),
        ylab = "% of all money raised", main = "Sources of House campaign money",
        legend.text = TRUE, args.legend = list(x = "topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.8))

Write about: these are shares of the total raised by each group, which is a different question from Part 4’s median candidate. Do the two tell the same story? Which is the fairer summary, and why might a journalist prefer one? Note what fills the gap for challengers where PAC money is absent — and what that implies about who can afford to run against a sitting member.

Option C — How big is the double-counting problem?

floor_amt <- 1000000              # <- change this

b <- fec[fec$ttl_receipts > floor_amt, ]
d <- table(b$ttl_receipts)
shared <- as.numeric(names(d[d > 1]))

c(candidates_above_floor = nrow(b),
  rows_sharing_a_total   = sum(b$ttl_receipts %in% shared),
  dollars_double_counted = round(sum(shared) / 1e6))
#> candidates_above_floor   rows_sharing_a_total dollars_double_counted

At some point matching on dollar amount stops finding real duplicates and starts finding coincidences — two candidates who each raised exactly $250,000, say. Option D — Ask your own question

Pick a state and look at everyone who ran in it. Compare the parties. Find the candidate with the most debt, or the most cash left over. Follow whatever nags.

What to submit. Knit to HTML or PDF and upload to Canvas, with your chosen chunk and two or three paragraphs of interpretation.

The writing is the assignment. I am not grading your code — it is my code. I am grading whether you can look at a ledger and say something true about who finances American politics.

Where the data came from

Federal Election Commission, bulk download, “All Candidates” file for the 2023–24 cycle (https://www.fec.gov/files/bulk-downloads/2024/weball24.zip), covering every candidate committee’s activity through 31 December 2024.

This is as close to an official source as anything in this course. It is a mandatory legal filing to a federal regulator, not a scrape or a compilation. That is worth registering after Week 2 — and it is also worth registering how much this authoritative file still cannot do. It does not say who won. It does not deduplicate candidates who change office mid-cycle. It does not distinguish money spent for a candidate by outside groups, which since Citizens United (2010) has become a very large share of what is actually spent on a race and appears nowhere in these rows.

Independent expenditures, super PACs and so-called dark money are all real, all enormous, and all outside this file. What you are looking at is the money that passed through the candidates’ own hands.

The script that downloaded, checked and trimmed this file is data/build-data.R. It prints its own sanity checks, including a count of the duplicate records that Part 6 is about — those are left in deliberately.
